title: Teaching Kubernetes which pod to delete
subtitle: When an LLM deployment scales down, Kubernetes removes a replica without knowing which one is holding the useful cache. This is my M.S. project, and it is not finished.
meta: M.S. project (CS 297) at San José State
Controller done, GPU benchmark still to run
Python, Kubernetes, vLLM, llm-d, k3s, Prometheus, Grafana
tldr: A small controller looks at each vLLM replica's cache, gives it a score, and writes that score into an annotation Kubernetes already understands. When the deployment shrinks, the replica with the least useful cache goes first.

sections.heading: Why this bothered me
body: LLM servers like vLLM keep a cache of prompts they have already worked through. If your request starts with the same system prompt as the last hundred requests, the server skips most of the work and answers quickly. If it does not have that prompt cached, it has to read the whole thing again from the top.
Here is the catch. Every replica has its own cache. Run three replicas and you get three different caches, a bit like three baristas who each remember a different set of regulars.

Now traffic drops at night, and the deployment goes from three replicas to two. Kubernetes has to fire one barista. It picks, roughly, the one who started most recently. It does not ask who knows the most regulars.

If the newest replica happens to hold the popular prompts, they are gone, and the next requests for them are slow until another replica learns them again. One time in three is bad enough odds that I wanted to fix it.

sections.heading: The lazy solution, which is the good one
body: My first instinct was to write something that watches for scale-downs and deletes the right pod itself. That means racing the part of Kubernetes whose whole job is deleting pods. I would lose that race, probably in production, probably on a Friday.

It turns out Kubernetes already has a knob for this. You can put an annotation called `pod-deletion-cost` on a pod, and when it has to choose, it deletes the cheapest one first. So the controller never deletes anything. It just keeps the price tags up to date and lets Kubernetes do what it was going to do anyway.

body.caption: Every 5 seconds: read each pod's cache metrics, work out a score, update the price tag if it changed enough.

body: The score itself is three lines:

body.code:
recent_hit_rate = hits_in_last_window / lookups_in_last_window
cache_value     = 0.7 * recent_hit_rate + 0.3 * kv_usage
deletion_cost   = round(cache_value * 1000)

body: A pod with a 70% hit rate ends up around 700. A pod with 5% ends up near 50. Guess which one goes.

sections.heading: Things I went back and forth on
body: Recent or lifetime hit rate? vLLM only gives you counters that go up forever, so a pod that was busy an hour ago and has done nothing since still looks great. I keep the previous reading for each pod and work out the rate between two scrapes, then smooth it so one noisy interval does not flip the ranking.

Why not just use how full the cache is? Because a cache full of prompts nobody asks for again is worth nothing. Hit rate tells you if the cache is useful, usage tells you how much there is to lose. I use both, weighted 0.7 and 0.3. Those weights are a judgment call. I have not tuned them yet.

How often to write? Kubernetes' own docs warn you not to update this annotation on every metric tick, because each update is a write to the API server. So I only write when the score has moved by at least 25. The ranking needs to be in the right order, not precise.
What if a scrape fails? The pod keeps its old score. Writing zero because of a network blip would be a great way to get the best pod deleted.

And for the comparison runs, turning the controller off is not enough. The old price tags would still be sitting on the pods and Kubernetes would still read them. The baseline has to strip the annotations too.

sections.heading: How I know it works so far
body: GPUs are expensive, so I built this as a ladder where the first rungs cost nothing.

body: Stages 1 and 2 run in CI on every push, with unit tests and a scale-in trial on a kind cluster. Stage 2 is the one I trust most right now: the cheapest pod is the one that gets removed.

sections.heading: The honest part

body.note: I have not run the GPU benchmark yet. Llama 3 8B on three A100 replicas is the plan. Until that is done I do not have a time-to-first-token number, and I would rather leave this section empty than put a guess in it.

body: What does exist: the controller, the scoring, the trial harness, an image that runs inside the cluster with the right permissions, dashboards in Grafana, and a script that runs the whole GPU day so I do not burn rented hours typing commands.

sections.heading: What I already know is wrong with it

list: The score can be up to 5 seconds old. A sudden traffic shift can beat it.
The annotation is best effort, and it only ranks pods inside one ReplicaSet.
Kubernetes looks at my cost before it thinks about spreading pods across nodes, so on a bigger cluster this could pile pods onto one node.
The 0.7 and 0.3 weights are my guess. A proper sweep is the obvious next experiment.

title: One click, one order
subtitle: How I built an order API that survives retries, and the bug in my first version that taught me the difference between checking and claiming.
meta: Deployed on AWS. Load tested on my laptop
Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis, ECS Fargate, RDS, Terraform, k6
tldr: Every order request carries an `Idempotency-Key`. The key is claimed in the same database transaction that creates the order, so two identical requests can never both create one. A retry gets the original answer back.

sections.heading: The problem everyone has met
body: You press Pay. The spinner spins. Nothing happens. You press Pay again. Did you just buy two?

From the server's side it is the same story. The client sends an order, the server saves it, and the reply gets lost on the way back. The client has no way to tell if the order went through, so the only sensible thing it can do is send it again. Without protection, that second request is a second order.
The usual answer is an idempotency key. The client sticks a unique key on the request, and the server promises that the same key always gives the same result. Try it:

sections.heading: My first version was wrong
body: I did the obvious thing. Look the key up. If it is not there, insert it and create the order. That works perfectly when requests arrive one at a time, which is exactly how they arrive when you test by hand.

Two requests with the same key at the same moment is a different story. Both look, both see nothing, both try to insert. One wins. The other crashes into the primary key and returns a 500. When I ran 50 parallel requests across 16 workers, 7 rounds out of 20 produced one.

The fix was to stop asking permission. Instead of checking and then inserting, the request just tries to claim the key, inside the same transaction as the order, and lets the database decide who got there first:

body.code:
INSERT INTO idempotency_records (...) VALUES (...)
ON CONFLICT (idem_key) DO UPDATE ... WHERE created_at < now() - <ttl>
RETURNING idem_key

body.caption: Request B waits on the unique index. When A commits, B gets zero rows back and reads A's stored answer instead.

body: If you get a row back, the key is yours and you create the order. If you get nothing, someone else owns it and you return their answer. And if the first request rolls back, the second one's insert goes through and it creates the order. There is no moment where both can.

sections.heading: Smaller decisions
body: Keys expire after 24 hours, which is plenty for retries. The claim query takes over an expired key on the spot, so expiry is exact even if the cleanup job has not run.
Cleanup takes a database lock so only one server does it per cycle. It deletes old keys and nothing else. Orders and ledger rows stay forever.

The rate limiter keeps its counts in Redis. My first one kept them in memory, which meant two servers each allowed the full limit. A limit of 10 that is really 20 is not much of a limit. If Redis goes down, the limiter lets requests through. I would rather be too generous than be down.
For the client's IP, I take the last entry of `X-Forwarded-For`, the one the load balancer adds. Everything before that is whatever the client felt like typing.

sections.heading: Then I made it fast
body: The first version opened a new database connection for every request, and the async handlers called a blocking driver directly. In practice, requests were queuing up and going one at a time. Moving the database calls to a threadpool and adding a connection pool changed things quite a bit:

body.note: I measured this with k6 on my laptop (an Apple M4), with the API, Postgres and k6 all on the same machine. It is a fair before and after. It is not what you would get in production, where every query also crosses a network.

body: The pool had one surprise in it. psycopg2's pool closes any connection handed back above its minimum size. With the default minimum of 1, a burst of traffic ended up reconnecting on almost every request, while holding the pool's lock. It was slower than having no pool at all, about 90 requests a second against 180. Setting the minimum equal to the maximum fixed it.

sections.heading: Where it runs

body.caption: All of it is Terraform, deployed by GitHub Actions.

body: The database migration runs every time a container starts. It is safe to run twice, and it takes a lock, so several containers booting at once do not trip over each other. There are 41 tests, and CI runs them on every push.
